analysis.one_liner: Caps direct federal student lending so loans keep flowing through banks and guaranty agencies.
analysis.headline: The bill, backed by its sponsor and 16 Republican cosponsors, was referred to the committee its sponsor chaired, never received a vote, and died when the 104th Congress ended in January 1997.
analysis.plain_summary: In 1995 the Clinton administration was scaling up direct federal student loans, in which the government lends money to students itself. This bill, led by Senator Nancy Kassebaum, would cap that program at 40 percent of new student loans, bar any new colleges from joining, and keep most loans flowing through the older guaranteed program, where private banks lend and guaranty agencies insure the loans for fees paid by taxpayers. The bill also adds some borrower-friendly features to the guaranteed program, like income-based repayment and an electronic application.
analysis.who_benefits: If passed, the main beneficiaries would be the guaranteed student loan industry: private lenders, guaranty agencies, and servicers that earn fees, subsidies, and insurance payments on every guaranteed loan. Students would gain a few added options in the guaranteed program, such as income-contingent repayment and cross-program consolidation.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Student loan banks and guaranty agencies

how_it_helps.text: Caps direct federal student loans at 40 percent of new loan volume from 1995-96 onward and forbids the Education Secretary from signing agreements with any additional colleges that had not joined the direct program by December 31, 1994, keeping the guaranteed loan program as the main channel.

Eliminates the statutory transition toward direct lending and requires that direct loans carry the same terms and conditions as guaranteed loans, so the two programs stay parallel rather than direct lending expanding on its own track.
Adds income-contingent repayment to the guaranteed loan program, letting borrowers in that program repay as a share of income.
Lets some borrowers consolidate across the two programs and permits electronic loan applications through guaranty agencies and lenders with no fee charged to applicants.

Requires detailed quarterly reports on the direct program's administrative spending and lets Congress control that spending through annual appropriations, which the bill's findings present as improved oversight.

analysis.who_pays: Students and taxpayers. Keeping the guaranteed program dominant means continuing the taxpayer-funded subsidies to lenders and guaranty agencies that direct lending was designed to bypass, and colleges that wanted to switch to direct lending would be frozen out.

drawbacks.text: The bill's own findings concede that Congress was being asked to rely on 'estimated budget savings which may prove illusory' about direct lending, yet the bill would cap the program precisely when it could be tested at scale, preserving the middleman subsidies the direct program was created to eliminate.

It freezes institutional choice: colleges that had not applied to the direct program by the end of 1994 could never join, locking in the guaranteed program's share of the market regardless of performance.

It conditions the Secretary's authority to make any new direct loans on issuing default-rate standards within 120 days, a mechanism that could halt the direct program entirely if the deadline were missed.

Its direct-consolidation fallback for guaranteed borrowers applies only when a lender cannot provide one, and the Secretary must withhold it if the Department lacks servicing capacity, limiting the practical relief offered to borrowers.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The borrower-facing additions (income-contingent repayment in the guaranteed program, cross-program consolidation, electronic applications) are real but modest, and parallel terms for direct loans are defensible. The bill's central effect, however, is to halt the growth of direct government lending and lock in a loan delivery system built on taxpayer subsidies to private intermediaries, whose cost to taxpayers was the very issue under debate. The oversight and reporting provisions are useful but do not offset the freeze on the alternative program.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and sent to the Senate Labor and Human Resources Committee, which its own sponsor chaired, and the committee never acted on it before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Senator Nancy Kassebaum introduced the bill on March 3, 1995, and it was read twice and referred to the Senate Committee on Labor and Human Resources.
Sixteen Republican senators cosponsored the bill; no Democrats did.
No further action appears in the record: the committee never reported the bill, the Senate never debated it, and it never received a vote before the 104th Congress ended on January 3, 1997.

The policy fight the bill embodied did not end there: that same year, Congress limited direct lending's growth through spending legislation, so the guaranteed loan industry's market position was partially protected even without this bill becoming law.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill died, the direct loan program was never capped or frozen by this legislation, which is the better outcome for colleges seeking the direct option and for taxpayers if direct lending is cheaper. The guaranteed loan industry nonetheless achieved much of what the bill sought through the year's appropriations battles, so the industry lost little either way.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Colleges and borrowers; industry gains came via riders

for.name: Sen. Nancy Kassebaum
for.role: Senator from Kansas and chair of the Senate Labor and Human Resources Committee
for.what_they_did: Sponsored the bill to cap direct lending and referred it to the committee she chaired, which never acted on it.

against.name: President Bill Clinton
against.what_they_did: The administration had made expansion of the direct student loan program a signature policy, which this bill was written to stop; no action by the administration on this specific bill appears in the record.

against.name: Guaranteed student loan industry (lenders, guaranty agencies, and servicers)
against.role: Banks and agencies in the Federal Family Education Loan program
against.what_they_did: Opposed expansion of direct lending, which bypassed their role as intermediaries; the bill was drafted to preserve their program.

sides.party_line_note: The sponsor and all 16 cosponsors were Republicans, with no Democratic cosponsors; the bill targeted a Clinton administration program, and no Senate Democrat supported it in any recorded action.

industries.industry: Guaranteed student loan industry (private lenders, guaranty agencies, and servicers)
industries.note: The bill caps the direct lending alternative at 40 percent of new volume, bars new colleges from joining it, and eliminates the transition toward direct lending, locking in the guaranteed program where lenders and guaranty agencies earn interest subsidies and administrative allowances funded by taxpayers. Its interest runs against students and taxpayers to the extent direct lending delivers loans at lower public cost.

Schools already accepted into the direct program could continue at the capped volume, but no new institution could ever join, removing schools' choice of delivery system; the bill also adds default-rate termination standards that apply to direct lending institutions.
